# Introduction

## Why Are We Here?

- [The Shift:]{.bold-hilit} Computation-based research is transitioning toward 
**Frictionless Reproducibility (FR)**. 

- [The Triad:]{.bold-hilit} FR driven by maturity of 3 data science principles: 
    + data sharing
    + code sharing
    + competitive challenges

- [The Superpower:]{.bold-hilit} Empirical Machine Learning (EML) uses this triad as an 
emergent superpower to drive AI progress.

- [The Export:]{.bold-hilit} These practices can be learned and adopted by *any* research 
field to instantly accelerate its rate of progress.


# Overview

## The Old Way vs. The New Way

The Old Way (In-Principle Sharing)

- A scientist publishes a paper with a beautiful chart. 
- If you want to check it, you have to email them, 
- Wait weeks for the data, 
- figure out their messy code, 
- and fix a dozen errors. 

## The Old Way vs. The New Way

The New Way (Frictionless Reproducibility)

- You read a paper, 
- click a link, 
- clone their GitHub repository, 
- and run their exact analysis on your laptop in 2 minutes. 

. . .


The "Singularity" 

When checking other people's data work becomes effortless, 
scientific progress explodes at breakneck speed.


## Cheap and Massive Compute Power

- [The Stalled Engine:]{.bold-hilit} Around 2005, individual computer chips stopped getting 
significantly faster year-over-year.

- [The Smartphone Boom:]{.bold-hilit} Because billions of people bought smartphones, 
tech companies built a massive global network of cloud servers to handle all that data.

- [The Result for Data Science:]{.bold-hilit} Today, any undergraduate student with a laptop can rent 
a supercomputer on the cloud for pennies to run massive datasets. 
Space and processing power are no longer bottlenecks.


## Data Science Matures

The Core Triad:

1. [Open Data:]{.bold-hilit} Exposing the raw numbers, not just summaries.
2. [Open Code:]{.bold-hilit} Sharing the exact scripts so others can re-run the math.
3. [Common Challenges:]{.bold-hilit} A shared goal where everyone uses the same dataset to compete for the best accuracy scores on a public leaderboard.

. . .

**Phase Transition:** When all three legs of the triad meet, researchers can reproduce 
or modify an outside institution's results within minutes or clicks.


## What Happens If You Hide One Leg?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### 🛑 No Challenges

- You get "Open Science" but no common goal. 
- Everyone works in isolated bubbles.
- Impossible to rank which method actually works best.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### 🛑 No Code

- You get competitions with secret methods (like the Netflix Prize). 
- People win, but no one learns *how* they won because the code is locked.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### 🛑 No Data

- You get "Bring-Your-Own-Data" science (like private medical trials). 
- You cannot verify the claims because the underlying data is a black box.
:::
::::


## Viral Science: Zero Friction

[The Meme Analogy]{.bold-hilit} <br>
Why do internet memes spread across the globe in a single afternoon? 
Because there is **zero friction** to share them—you just click "forward." 

- [Viral Code:]{.bold-hilit} When data, code, and leaderboards are completely open, 
scientific ideas spread through a research community exactly like viral memes.

- [The "URL or I Don't Care" Rule:]{.bold-hilit} Modern data analysts reject paywalls 
and broken links. If a research method doesn't have an immediate, working link, 
the community ignores it and moves on.


## Automated Science Tracking

- [Code as Gold:]{.bold-hilit} In the future, public code repositories will be treated as raw material. 

- [Automated Tweaking:]{.bold-hilit} Data scientists will write automated scripts designed 
to crawl through thousands of *past* papers, pull down their code, and automatically 
swap parameters to find hidden improvements.

- [The Backwater Risk:]{.bold-hilit} Research fields that refuse to share their data and 
code due to privacy or copyright fears will be left behind and forgotten by the next generation.

## Debate

. . .

Going back to LeVeque's "Theorems Without Proofs" analogy, publication of theorems without
proofs is not acceptable. Yet, we accept computational outputs without the code that 
produce them.

. . .

::: {.poll}
Why does the scientific community tolerate this double standard?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(2, bottom = 0)
```

::: {.notes}
Is a computer script fundamentally different from a mathematical proof, 
or are we just living in a scientifically immature era of computing?
:::


## Debate

<!-- Protect Your Output vs. Public Provenance -->

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 🛡️ The Pragmatist View

It took me three years to write this algorithmic base. If I open-source it now, my 
competitors will use my code to publish five papers before I can even finish my next draft.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 🌐 The Open View

Publicly archiving your code with a timestamped DOI is the absolute best way to 
claim ownership, establish provenance, and legally force competitors to cite you.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.poll}
If you are a funding agency, how do you balance a scientist's valid right to profit 
from their multi-year software labor against the public's right to verify the data 
pipeline immediately?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(4, bottom = 0)
```


## Debate

<!-- The Fear of Maintenance -->

Many researchers hide their scripts because they are terrified that once the 
code is public, their inbox will be flooded with emails from strangers asking 
for technical troubleshooting, custom modifications, or software installation help.

. . .

::: {.poll}
How do you draw a boundary between providing necessary scientific transparency 
and protecting your personal time from being hijacked by outside users demanding 
free tech support?
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3, bottom = 0)
```

::: {.notes}
Barnes and LeVeque emphasize that research code is a static archive of a publication, 
not a commercial product that comes with customer support. 
:::
